title: What happened at the close
text: Stocks ended the week a little lower. The S&P 500 fund SPY lost 0.5% on Friday to $759.97, and the Nasdaq 100 fund QQQ ended almost flat at $704.40. Energy was the strongest group on the Nasdaq, up 3.1%, while consumer staples lagged. Next week is busy: the Fed meets on Wednesday and Alphabet reports its results on October 28, so prices may swing. This is information for learning, not advice.

title: GE fell even after good news
text: GE Aerospace closed at $285.64, down 2.7%, and sits 26.5% below its 52 week high. Earlier this week it reported profit above what analysts expected and raised its yearly forecast, yet the stock still dropped. The average analyst price target is $385.71, about 35.0% above the price. A price target is just an opinion about where a stock might go in a year, so treat it as one clue.

title: Eli Lilly slips from near its high
text: Eli Lilly closed at $1,273.46, down 2.5%, but it is still only 3.6% below its 52 week high of $1,321.21. The dividend fund SCHD closed at $35.27, just 0.5% below its high. A stock near its high has already risen a lot, so a small drop is easier to notice. That is not good or bad by itself.

title: Chip stocks bounce but are still low
text: AMD rose 1.7% and TSMC rose 1.5%, a small bounce after Thursday's fall. Even so, Vertiv is 48.9% below its 52 week high and Broadcom is 35.0% below. A stock that has fallen far can swing a lot in both directions, and that swing is what the risk score measures.

title: Lesson 21: What is the Federal Reserve?
text: The Federal Reserve, often called the Fed, is the central bank of the United States. One of its main jobs is to set a key interest rate that affects how much it costs to borrow money. When the Fed raises rates, loans like mortgages and car loans usually get more expensive, and bonds often pay more. When it lowers rates, borrowing gets cheaper. Stocks often react because company profits and investor moods change with the cost of money. The Fed meets several times a year and announces its decision, and investors watch every word. Next week the Fed meets again, which is why markets can feel jumpy beforehand. The Fed does not tell anyone what to buy or sell, and this is for learning, not advice to buy or sell anything.
